validator: draft 1 passes validate.mjs with no hard problems, soft points or warnings. The faults below are the critic's, not the validator's.
keep: The idea is named up front: lesson 1's ratios stopped at 90°, and a turning arm carries them to every angle.

The circle is built from lesson 1's triangle with a hypotenuse of 1 (Weber's constructing group, brief notes 6.1), so (cos θ, sin θ) follows from opposite ÷ 1 and adjacent ÷ 1 rather than being handed over; the point itself is cited to OpenStax [1].
Negative values come from where the tip is, not from a sign rule to learn; the quadrant signs are read off the picture and cited to Bitesize [2].

sin² θ + cos² θ = 1 is shown as Pythagoras on the arm, with sin² θ = (sin θ)² said once, and tan θ = sin θ ÷ cos θ as the arm's slope, undefined at 90° like an upright line in Straight-line graphs. Both are derived on screen, so no source is needed for them.
The level line gives two angles with the same sine by mirror symmetry, sin (180° − θ) = sin θ, and the calculator's single answer is set beside it (MCA 5.1.8; prepares lesson 4's ambiguous case).

Twelve screens: SHOW 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 alternate with DO 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, and two mixed puzzles close (11 a negative sine with both angles, 12 cos 110° for lesson 4's Cambridge slip). Each puzzle has three answers whose wrong ones are named slips.
Every lesson-3 misconception in the brief has a puzzle: x as sine (screen 2 at 40°, Williams [3]), one answer only (screens 10 and 11), the negative cosine (screens 4 and 12).

Every number is assumed, computed from the shown rule or a cited constant, and all were recomputed: cos/sin at 30, 40, 120, 150, 210, 300, 330 and 110°, sin⁻¹ 0.8 = 53.1°, sin⁻¹ 0.3 = 17.5°, tan 150° = −0.577, 0.2 × cos 30° = 0.173.
fix: False absolute: 'For angles from 0° to 90° this gives lesson 1's values' includes 0° and 90°, where there is no triangle. Say 'between 0° and 90°'.
False absolute: practice's level-line step says the line crosses at the angle and at 180° minus it; at sin θ = 1 or −1 these are one angle. Add that at the very top or bottom the two are one angle.

Unsourced conventions stated as plain fact: the name 'supplementary' and the numbering of quadrants anticlockwise from the top right are textbook conventions with no quote in RESEARCH. Word them as textbook usage, as the reflex angle already is.

Causal step skipped: the explanation says beyond 90° the across-and-up rule 'is how sine and cosine are defined' without saying why that choice: it is the one rule that agrees with lesson 1 inside the first quadrant and needs no triangle to work. Add the reason in a clause.
Unreadable picture risk at 340 px: screen 9 puts a calculator 'beside' the circle with two arms, two angle labels, the level line and three readouts. Put the calculator below the circle.
Analogy wording: 'once it passes the far side it is below the axle' is vague about where the knob is. Say it moves to the other side over the top and drops below the axle round the far side.

faults.causal step skipped: one: why the across-and-up rule is the definition past 90° (fixed above). The mirror argument for sin (180° − θ) and Pythagoras for the squares each give their reason.
faults.false absolutes: two: '0° to 90°' including the ends, and 'crosses twice' at the very top and bottom in practice. 'Squaring takes the signs away, so it holds in every quadrant' and 'sin⁻¹ gives only one angle, between −90° and 90°' hold everywhere.
faults.interactive shows effect, not cause: none: dragging the arm moves the tip, and the readouts are the tip's own across and up, with the triangle drawn under the arm; the level line shows the mirror pair that causes two answers.
faults.checks test recall: none: there are no checks in read mode; the puzzles ask him to use the picture (read a sine off a point, sign by quadrant, the second angle).
faults.thin or decorative research: none: [1] carries the point (cos θ, sin θ), [2] the quadrant signs, [3] the slip, [4] the ratios, [10] degrees mode, [11] the full turn. The identity and tan = sin ÷ cos are derived on screen rather than cited, as the brief allows ('The picture shows the identity from Pythagoras either way').
faults.unreadable labels: one: the calculator on screen 9 (fixed above). The two coordinate readouts sit on their own axes, sine on the up axis, as the brief asks for Williams' slip.
faults.talks about the idea instead of teaching: none: every paragraph works a value on the arm.

shape.rule stated in words: yes (cosine across, sine up; the second angle with the same sine is 180° minus the first)
shape.one fully worked example with real numbe: yes (150°, 0.75 + 0.25 = 1, sin θ = 0.8 giving 53.1° and 126.9°; practice: sin θ = 0.3 and −0.3)
shape.misconception shown failing: yes (x as sine, 360° − θ giving −0.8, cos 110° without its sign)
shape.analogy from his trade with where it bre: yes (a cable drum's handle; breaks on the handle's length and on whole turns)
shape.put it into practice: yes (steps, rule of thumb, worked example, mistakes)

left_out: The general solution of trig equations and angles past 360° are left out (brief: the full general solution waits for college); one clause in ignores says turning past a full turn brings the same arm round. Two angles with the same cosine (θ and 360° − θ) appear only as the slip in the 360° − θ mistake, to keep the lesson on the sine, which lesson 4 needs.
